---
title: "Agnes Greenway, New Westminster: Indigenous art in pavement"
description: "A TrafficPatterns install at the Agnes Greenway in New Westminster, a design by Rain Pierre of Katzie First Nation, fused into the greenway pavement."
date: "2023-06-12"
author: "Square One Paving"
category: "Public Art"
featured_image: "/images/applications/parks-paths/eagle-mural-courtyard-aerial-01.jpg"
tags: ["Agnes Greenway", "New Westminster", "TrafficPatterns", "Rain Pierre", "Katzie First Nation", "reconciliation"]
---

The Agnes Greenway is a pedestrian and cycling corridor running through New Westminster, connecting downtown residential streets to the city's broader active-transportation network. In June 2023 we installed a pavement art piece along the greenway, designed by Rain Pierre, an artist from the Katzie First Nation.

The installation anchors a stretch of the greenway adjacent to École Qayqayt, a school that carries its Halkomelem name as a daily act of acknowledgement. The pavement art continues that acknowledgement in physical form, underfoot, for every student and resident who uses the corridor.

## The artist

Rain Pierre is a Katzie First Nation artist whose work spans carving, painting, and increasingly, applied public art. His designs carry the visual vocabulary of his nation (form lines, animal figures, ancestral symbols), adapted for the scale and material of the site.

When a Katzie artist's work is installed on Katzie territory (New Westminster sits within traditional Katzie lands, shared historically with other Coast Salish nations), the artwork does something that no imported design can do. It marks the ground as the ground the community has always walked.

## The product

We installed the design in TrafficPatterns preformed thermoplastic. The product is engineered for high-pedestrian and low-to-moderate vehicular traffic, which matches the Agnes Greenway use profile: continuous foot and cycle traffic, occasional service-vehicle access, four-season weather exposure.

TrafficPatterns sheets are pre-cut from the artist's artwork at full installation scale. The install process is torch-down. The asphalt and the sheet reach bonding temperature together, and the material fuses into the substrate as it cools. The marking is not a coating. It is part of the pavement.

Expected service life at a greenway site with the Agnes Greenway's traffic profile is in the seven-to-ten-year window at full colour saturation, with gradual softening past that. For civic art attached to an ongoing reconciliation commitment, that service life matters: the artwork doesn't disappear after one winter.

## The École Qayqayt connection

École Qayqayt, the elementary school that anchors the greenway, is named using the Halkomelem name for the land the school is built on. The school's daily practice of centring that name inside student life is a quiet form of reconciliation work, and Rain Pierre's pavement piece complements that work directly.

Students at Qayqayt walk across the installation on their way to school. They ask questions about it. The design enters the visual vocabulary of their daily commute. Over years, that repeated encounter is the kind of exposure that shifts what a community considers normal, and what becomes normal is acknowledgement of the land's first people, rendered as a civic fact rather than a ceremonial gesture.

## The install

Greenway installs have their own operational profile. The corridor stays open for pedestrians where possible: we work in staged sections, closing a section at a time rather than the whole greenway, so the corridor remains functional throughout.

Asphalt preparation on this site was straightforward: the pavement was in good condition, and the substrate accepted the thermoplastic cleanly. Layout was surveyed from reference points the city provided, and we ran the torch-down application in the window between early morning pedestrian traffic and the evening cycling peak.

Colour matching was done against the artist's specification sheets and confirmed with sample panels before the full install proceeded.

## What the greenway does now

Since the install, the Agnes Greenway reads as a curated civic corridor rather than as a piece of transportation infrastructure. The art brings an intentionality to the route that a plain asphalt path couldn't carry.

In New Westminster, the installation connects to the city's broader reconciliation and placemaking commitments: the Qayqayt school name, the Every Child Matters installation elsewhere in the city, the ongoing work with local Nations on public-realm visibility.

For us as installers, the Agnes Greenway is the kind of work that expands what a pavement studio can be. We are not only marking lanes and paving parking lots. We are carrying the work of artists and Nations into the physical substrate of the community.

If your municipality is planning a greenway, corridor, or plaza install with First Nations partnership, [get in touch](/contact). We have done this category of work across the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island, and we take it seriously every time we are asked.

title: "Alexandra Greenway, Richmond: DuraTherm public art by Bagua Artist Association"
description: "Public art on the Alexandra Greenway in Richmond, a Bagua Artist Association design in DuraTherm thermoplastic, inlaid flush into imprinted asphalt."
date: "2021-11-30"
author: "Square One Paving"
category: "Public Art"
featured_image: "/images/applications/parks-paths/eagle-mural-courtyard-aerial-01.jpg"
tags: ["DuraTherm", "Richmond", "public art", "greenway", "community", "thermoplastic", "pathway", "stamped asphalt", "Bagua Artist Association"]
---

The Alexandra Greenway in Richmond is a community public art and beautification project created in partnership with the Bagua Artist Association. The installation uses DuraTherm, a design-flexible and durable preformed thermoplastic material, inlaid into imprinted asphalt to create a lasting surface artwork along the greenway corridor.

This is the type of project that demonstrates what's possible when public art and surface engineering work together rather than in parallel. The artistic design was developed by the Bagua Artist Association; the surface engineering was our responsibility. The result is a greenway surface that is both a pedestrian pathway and a public artwork.

## DuraTherm for complex art installations

DuraTherm is the product we specify when the design complexity exceeds what StreetBond® coatings can achieve. Where StreetBond is excellent for broad colour fields and geometric patterns, DuraTherm allows us to work with intricate design elements: the kind of detail that an artist's design typically demands.

The preformed thermoplastic is manufactured to exact CAD specifications, then thermally inlaid into the asphalt substrate during installation. The material sits at the same level as the surrounding asphalt, not raised above it, which means it doesn't create a trip hazard and doesn't peel at the edges over time.

## The systems

Square One installs DuraTherm under our [preformed thermoplastic](/services/preformed-thermoplastic) service. The manufacturer's published facts: a thermoplastic pavement marking applied by inset or surface methods, on asphalt or concrete; retroreflective; made to TAC shapes and legends for its road-marking work; resistant to BC freeze-thaw cycles; and a service life well beyond painted markings. The inset method is what matters on a greenway: it is how the thermoplastic ends up flush with the imprinted asphalt around it rather than proud of it. The imprinting itself is [stamped asphalt](/services/stamped-asphalt): a heated template pressed into the surface, so the texture is in the pavement rather than on it. Specifications are on the [DuraTherm product page](/products/duratherm); the [public art gallery](/applications/public-art) shows artwork rendered in thermoplastic and coatings across BC.

## Public art in the civic realm

The Alexandra Greenway project represents a model worth noting: community artist organizations, municipal parks departments, and specialized surface installation contractors working together to create public art that is also functional infrastructure.

The Bagua Artist Association's design is the cultural and creative content. DuraTherm is the delivery mechanism that ensures that content survives BC's climate over a multi-year timeframe.

Greenways are a recurring setting for this kind of work in our record. The [Agnes Greenway in New Westminster](/blog/agnes-greenway-new-westminster) carries a TrafficPatterns™ design by Rain Pierre of Katzie First Nation, and the concourse at [Joyce SkyTrain Station](/blog/joyce-skytrain-art-installation) carries Renée Van Halm's "Carpeting" in StreetBond, three materials, one principle: the artwork is in the surface, not on it.

## For a parks department or artist collective

- **Pick the material by the artwork.** Fine line and lettering suit inset thermoplastic; broad colour suits coating; a stamped texture gives either something to sit in. Many pieces use more than one.
- **Design for feet and wheels.** A greenway carries strollers, bikes and wheelchairs; flush inlay and anti-skid finishes keep the art from becoming an obstacle.
- **Proof at full scale.** The cut file is the artwork's last edit; a full-size print on the path before cutting catches what a screen cannot.

For public art projects requiring durable surface installation across BC, send the artwork and a photo of the site, or a postal code, to [office@squareonepaving.com](mailto:office@squareonepaving.com), call 604-612-6209, or use the [contact form](/contact). We come out, look, and put a written quote together.

title: "Boundary Road Pump Station: a StreetBond quilt motif on a utility site"
description: "A StreetBond quilt motif in eight colours wrapping the plaza, paths and steps at the Boundary Road pump station, a utility site that reads as public art."
date: "2024-01-09"

---

Utility infrastructure sites (pump stations, electrical substations, water treatment facilities) are a feature of every municipality. They're functional, they're necessary, and they're typically either invisible (enclosed in buildings) or visually unremarkable where they break the surface.

The Boundary Road pump station project took a different approach: using StreetBond® coatings in a quilt motif pattern to turn the surface around the installation into something that contributes to the neighbourhood streetscape.

## What the photograph shows

The lede photograph is the site from above, on a clear day. A field of large squares in eight colours (red, yellow, two blues, white, black, magenta and pink) fills the plaza around the pump station, runs to the edge of the road at the three-way stop, and wraps the steps down to the path beyond. Timber benches and a line of bollards sit on the pattern, and the pump station building itself carries the same colours, with a yellow gate. Behind it an elevated guideway crosses the frame, which is exactly the kind of setting that usually gets a chain-link fence and a gravel apron. The [project record](/projects/boundary-road-pump-station) holds two more frames, including the steps.

## Utility beautification as community investment

The quilt motif is a design choice with specific cultural resonance: quilt patterns are part of the textile heritage of many communities, and the grid-based geometry of a quilt translates effectively into pavement surface design.

Applied in StreetBond to the pump station site, the quilt pattern accomplishes several things:

1. **It signals care**: a utility site that has been treated with a designed surface is a utility site that the operator has thought about. That signals something to the neighbourhood.
2. **It creates visual interest**: a well-executed quilt pattern at ground level is genuinely engaging. Pedestrians passing the site see something worth noticing rather than plain utility infrastructure.
3. **It establishes precedent**: utility sites across a municipality that have been given similar design attention create a consistent civic character. The investment in one site argues for investment in others.

## The technical application

The quilt pattern was laid out in StreetBond using multiple colours. The geometry of a quilt pattern is precise: the grid has to be consistent and the colour zones have to be clean-edged. We use CAD-referenced layout on installations like this to ensure the geometry is correct before the coating crew begins. The stairs take the pattern as well as the flat.

## The system

Square One installs StreetBond under our [decorative coatings](/services/decorative-coatings) service. The manufacturer's published facts: a water-based acrylic pavement coating that bonds to asphalt and to concrete, with the appropriate primer for each; more than 50 standard colours plus custom mixing, which is how a quilt gets eight of them; an anti-skid aggregate for wet surfaces; a UV-stable finish; and an 8+ year life cycle, refreshed rather than replaced. The [StreetBond product page](/products/streetbond) has the specification, and the [public art gallery](/applications/public-art) holds the wider record of artwork rendered in the surface itself.

## For a utility or municipality

- **Treat the apron as public realm.** The ground around a pump station is a plaza whether or not anyone designs it; a pattern turns the leftover into a place.
- **Design on a grid.** A quilt, a checkerboard or a stripe survives the geometry of curbs, steps and equipment pads; a free-form mural fights them.
- **Carry the colours up the walls.** The Boundary Road station's building shares the palette of its plaza, which is why the site reads as one piece rather than a painted floor beside a grey box.

For municipalities and utilities considering beautification programs for infrastructure sites, send a photo of the site and a postal code to [office@squareonepaving.com](mailto:office@squareonepaving.com), call 604-612-6209, or use the [contact form](/contact). Snug Cove is the heart of Bowen Island: the ferry landing, the commercial area, the place where the island community gathers. We were engaged to install a public art feature at the cove using StreetBond® 150 coatings on the walkway surface.

The brief was straightforward in its intent and demanding in its execution: create something that represents the community, holds up to Bowen Island's marine climate, and reads as considered public art rather than decorative maintenance.

## What the photograph shows

The lede photograph is a close look at one stretch of the walkway. Ovals of colour (yellow, green, blue and a warm grey) are scattered across the asphalt like stepping stones, and in one blue oval a seal looks up at a speech bubble beside it that reads "I wish this were a water slide!" The joke is the point: each colour in the design stands for part of the island community, and the local wildlife asks the questions. The lettering and the seal are as crisp as the ovals, which is the difference between coating and paint. The [project record](/projects/bowen-island-snug-cove-walkway) holds a second, wider frame of the walkway.

## Community branding in surface design

The colour palette for this installation was developed with the community context in mind. Each of the custom colours in the design represents something specific to the island: its character, its natural environment, its identity as a distinct community accessible only by ferry.

This is the category of work we call community branding: surfaces that do more than protect the pavement underneath. The finished walkway at Snug Cove is the first thing visitors see arriving from the ferry, and the daily backdrop for residents who walk it year-round.

## StreetBond 150 in a marine environment

Bowen Island's proximity to the water means any surface system has to perform in salt air, high humidity, and the freeze-thaw cycles that BC island climates deliver. StreetBond 150 is our specification for these conditions: the formulation is designed for outdoor Canadian applications, and the aggregate embed provides slip resistance on a surface that will be wet for months at a time.

Application is direct to the existing asphalt and concrete substrate. The prep work (cleaning, profiling, priming where required) is the foundation of a coating that lasts. We mobilized our crew to Bowen Island via ferry for this install, which we do regularly for island communities across BC.

## The system

Square One installs StreetBond under our [decorative coatings](/services/decorative-coatings) service; 150 is the standard coating, and StreetBond SR is the solar-reflective version. Brewers Park in Burnaby was due for a playground surface renewal. The existing asphalt was functional but grey, a missed opportunity to make the space more engaging for the families who use it daily.

We installed StreetBond® coatings across the playground's asphalt surface, using a colourful multi-zone design that turns the functional surface into an active part of the playground experience.

## Playground surfaces and StreetBond

Playground asphalt surfaces have to perform across a wide range of demands. Children are not gentle with surfaces: running, jumping, bike-riding and scooter use are all in scope. The surface needs to be safe (consistent traction, no sharp edges or lifted material), bright (colour that stays strong rather than chalking and fading), and durable enough to function for years without recoating.

StreetBond delivers on all three counts. The aggregate embed provides consistent slip resistance. The colour formulation is UV-stable, designed for outdoor Canadian applications where months of high summer UV alternate with wet winters. And the bond to the asphalt substrate means the coating doesn't lift at edges or peel under vehicle or foot traffic.

The Brewers Park installation uses multiple StreetBond colours in a zoned layout: creating distinct play areas that read as designed spaces rather than utilitarian infrastructure.

## The park context

Brewers Park was undergoing broader improvements at the time of our installation, with increased community use expected as the surrounding area developed. A playground with a well-designed surface signals that the park operator has invested in the space, and that signal matters for community perception and use patterns.

## The system

Square One installs StreetBond under our [decorative coatings](/services/decorative-coatings) service. The manufacturer's published facts: a water-based acrylic pavement coating that works on asphalt and concrete, with an anti-skid aggregate for wet surfaces, more than 50 standard colours plus custom mixing, and a UV-stable finish. The manufacturer rates it at an 8+ year life cycle and describes the end of that cycle as a refresh rather than a replacement: the colour is recoated over the existing surface, and the asphalt underneath stays put. The [StreetBond product page](/products/streetbond) has the specification.

## The same coating, three ways, in the same region

---
title: "Commercial parking lots: why a coating lasts where paint fails"
description: "Parking lot markings take more abuse than almost any other surface. Here's what holds up on a BC commercial site, and what doesn't."
date: "2026-02-05"
author: "Square One Paving"
category: "Commercial"
featured_image: "/images/applications/parking-lots/mission-parking-bays-and-lot-streetprint-01.jpg"
tags: ["parking lots", "preformed thermoplastic", "decorative coatings", "commercial", "Langford"]
---

A commercial parking lot is one of the hardest working surfaces on any property. Every car that arrives rolls over the same twenty square metres near the entrance. Delivery trucks turn tight radius on the same inside corner. Snow and salt accumulate in the same four depressions. Then the spring thaw hits and all of it gets exposed at once.

We installed the full markings and accessible-parking graphics at Westshore Town Centre in Langford a few years back: TrafficPatterns preformed thermoplastic, custom arrows, stall markings, and the accessible-parking graphics in blue and white. The markings are still holding. The white lines painted by the general contractor before we arrived? Those are mostly gone.

Here's what separates the two outcomes.

## Paint is a one-season solution

A conventional traffic-paint stall line lays down roughly 300 microns thick. On a flat, low-traffic surface that might last eighteen months. In a commercial parking lot with freeze-thaw exposure, snow clearing, and daily vehicle traffic over the same spots, you're looking at six to nine months before visible fading and another six before the lines are unreadable.

Most property managers handle this with an annual repaint. That's an operational cost that just repeats every spring. Over a ten-year facility lifecycle, the total spend on paint exceeds what a thermoplastic install would have cost up front.

## Thermoplastic is structural

Preformed thermoplastic bonds into the asphalt. The markings are typically 2–3mm thick with reflective glass beads embedded through the full depth. When a snowplow scrapes over one, the top of the marking wears, not the bond. The reflective beads that were below the surface become the new surface.

Durability in a lot context usually runs five to seven years for stall lines and seven to ten for higher-thickness applications like directional arrows.

## Where decorative coatings come in

Some commercial sites want more than function. A mixed-use development, a premium retail plaza, or a hotel approach wants the parking area to read as part of the architecture, not as an afterthought.

That's where a StreetBond coating earns its place. We've coated drive lanes, accessible-parking fields, and pedestrian crossings inside lots in deep grey, warm terracotta, and a slate tone that reads as natural stone from a distance. The coating slip-resistance is graded for vehicle traffic, and the colour range is specified for UV stability in North American conditions, meaning it doesn't fade to pink the way off-spec pigments do after two summers.

Coated zones inside a lot also reduce driver speed. The visual transition registers as a different kind of space. Customers slow automatically when they cross into a coloured pedestrian zone. That's a safety outcome you don't get from paint.

## Accessibility compliance, done once

BC accessibility requirements for parking (stall dimensions, international-symbol-of-accessibility placement, loading-zone striping, connecting accessible routes to building entries) are specific, and they change as provincial regulations update.

We install the accessibility package in preformed thermoplastic with the correct blue pigment, correct symbol sizing, and correct edge-of-stall tactile markings where required. A repaint cycle using the wrong symbol proportions or the wrong colour is a compliance problem, not just a cosmetic one.

## When it's worth the upgrade

The case for thermoplastic and coatings over paint is strongest in three situations: lots that see heavy daily volume (retail, medical, institutional), lots exposed to snow clearing, and lots that are part of a premium development where the surface is part of the brand.

If the lot is low-traffic, sheltered, and rarely sees freeze-thaw, paint is fine. Everywhere else, it's just a maintenance cost compounding year over year.

We specify and install parking-lot markings and coatings across the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island. [Get in touch for a commercial scope review](/contact) if you're budgeting for a 2026 or 2027 lot refresh.

blog.crosswalk-art-public-installations-bc.md:
---
title: "When a crosswalk is public art"
description: "Decorative crosswalks in Vancouver and Nanaimo. How a stamped asphalt install becomes civic identity, and what the engineering actually looks like."
date: "2026-01-08"
author: "Square One Paving"
category: "Municipal"
featured_image: "/images/applications/crosswalks/delta-gateway-casino-brick-crossing-trafficpatterns-01.jpg"
tags: ["crosswalks", "stamped asphalt", "public art", "StreetPrint", "Nanaimo", "Vancouver"]
---

A few summers back we installed a set of crosswalks in the Nanaimo waterfront district as part of a public-realm upgrade. The brief called for decorative stamped asphalt with a marine-themed pattern, tied into the wider harbourfront redesign. What we ended up with was a crosswalk that functions as both traffic control and civic identity, and that's the category this kind of work actually belongs in.

We also installed a downtown Vancouver crosswalk upgrade around the same time with a more traditional brick stamp and a retroreflective finish. Two projects, two very different briefs, same underlying product.

This piece is about what goes into a crosswalk like that, and why cities across BC are asking for them now instead of five years ago.

## The shift toward decorative crosswalks

A generation ago, a crosswalk was four white stripes and that was the end of the conversation. The shift since then has been driven by two things: pedestrian-safety research and placemaking strategy.

The safety side is straightforward. A visually distinct crosswalk registers earlier in a driver's peripheral vision than a standard ladder-pattern crosswalk. The visual pattern break (brick, cobblestone, ashlar) reads as information-dense. Drivers approach with more attention.

The placemaking side is the more recent driver. Cities in BC are rethinking their main streets as destinations, not through-corridors. A distinctive crosswalk is one of the cheapest interventions that signals to a visitor: you are somewhere specific now. The pavement becomes part of the brand of the district.

## The engineering under the pattern

What makes a decorative crosswalk durable under real traffic is the product choice, not the pattern design.

We use StreetPrint: stamped into fresh, hot asphalt with heavy-duty metal templates, then coated with StreetBond for colour and UV stability. The stamping happens in a narrow temperature window while the asphalt is still workable. Too cool and the impression is shallow. Too hot and the template distorts.

Once stamped and cooled, the surface is structurally identical to standard asphalt. A bus crosses it. A snowplow scrapes it. Winter freeze-thaw cycles work it up and down. None of that damages the pattern because the pattern isn't a coating: it's a three-dimensional impression in the asphalt itself.

The StreetBond coating over top carries the colour. It's UV-stable to a published specification, and when it dulls it is recoated rather than replaced.

## Retroreflective finishes are a real upgrade

The downtown Vancouver crosswalk we did had a retroreflective finish: glass beads embedded in the surface layer that return headlight beams back to their source at night.

In a night-time pedestrian environment, that's the difference between a crosswalk that becomes a hazard after 9pm and one that stays readable. Vehicle headlights illuminate the retroreflective beads, the beads return that light, and the entire pattern outline registers from fifty metres out.

This is not a cosmetic upgrade. It's a specification decision that shapes whether the crosswalk performs in the conditions it actually needs to perform in.

## What cities ask us about

Most of the conversations we have with planners and streetscape designers at BC municipalities land on the same few questions:

How long does a decorative crosswalk last? In BC conditions, fifteen to twenty years with a mid-life coating refresh around year ten. The underlying stamped asphalt holds longer than that.

How does it compare in cost to four-stripe paint? Ten to fifteen times more expensive on install. Roughly comparable on twenty-year total cost, because four-stripe paint is a three-year rewrite cycle.

Can it carry snowplows? Yes. StreetPrint is designed for plow equipment and we install it specifically in climates that use plows.

Can we use it at a signalized intersection with heavy truck traffic? Yes. We've installed at exactly those conditions. The key is using the correct asphalt mix under the stamp and specifying the right coating over it.

## If you're planning one

The planning stage is where a good decorative crosswalk gets built. Pattern selection, colour palette, how the crosswalk ties into adjacent sidewalk treatments, and how it coordinates with signage: those decisions are made in design, not on install day.

We work with municipal engineering teams and landscape architects across BC on crosswalk specifications, and we're happy to come in early in a project to provide material and install input. [Get in touch if you're scoping a public-realm upgrade](/contact).

On September 22, 2023, in the lead-up to the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, we installed an Every Child Matters pavement application in New Westminster. The design came from Charliss Santos, the 2023 winner of the national Every Child Matters T-shirt design contest. The install was made possible through the Orange Shirt Society, the municipality, and the Spirit of Children Society.

I want to write about this one because the work was the kind that a pavement studio should be honoured to be asked to do.

## The design and the designer

Charliss Santos's winning design was selected in 2023 from submissions across the country. The design carries the weight of a movement that began with Phyllis Webstad's story in 2013 and has become, every September 30, a nationally observed acknowledgement of the residential school system and the children who did not come home.

When a design like this is chosen for permanent pavement installation, the choice of product isn't a commercial decision. It's a question of whether the surface will carry the artwork forward faithfully: whether the edges will hold, whether the colours will stay true, whether the design will still read clearly in 2030 the way the artist intended it in 2023.

## TrafficPatterns for a ceremonial install

We installed this piece in TrafficPatterns preformed thermoplastic. The reasoning is the same reasoning that applies to every civic installation of cultural weight: the material has to hold the design without compromise across its full service life, and it has to fuse to the substrate in a way that no coating-over-paint approach can match.

TrafficPatterns sheets are pre-cut from the artist's CAD artwork. The installation happens in a single heat cycle: the asphalt and the sheet are brought to bonding temperature simultaneously, and the two fuse as they cool. The finished surface is structurally part of the pavement. It does not peel. It does not lift. It does not fade unevenly at the edges.

Expected service life in the New Westminster climate for this colour spec is in the five-to-seven-year window at full saturation, with gradual softening after that. For an installation tied to a national day of observance, that service life means the community engages with the artwork, in its original colours, for the better part of a decade.

## The sponsors

The install was funded through a partnership between the Orange Shirt Society (the national organization founded on Phyllis Webstad's story), the municipality, and the Spirit of Children Society (a New Westminster non-profit supporting Indigenous and at-risk children in the community). The Orange Shirt Society provides the national design contest framework. The municipality commits the civic space. The Spirit of Children Society connects the work to the community it most directly serves.

That kind of layered sponsorship is how a ceremonial install of this scale comes together. No single actor carries it. The design, the funding, the civic space, and the install expertise each come from a different source, and they align because the shared purpose makes them align.

## What the surface does on September 30

On the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, residents of New Westminster walk across the design on their way to events, to schools, to the ceremonies that happen across the community that week. The design is not a poster that gets taken down. It is not a video that stops playing. It is part of the city, underfoot, every day of the year, and on September 30, the design is the ground that the observance stands on.

That permanence is what separates a pavement install from other forms of public-facing design. The surface is always there. It acknowledges what it acknowledges, every day, and the community does not need to be reminded to remember because the ground itself is the reminder.

Square One's role on a project like this is narrow and important. We do not design the artwork. We do not fund the work. We do not determine the civic meaning. What we do is translate the design into a surface that will carry that meaning forward faithfully across the service life the community paid for.

On the Charliss Santos design, the install was clean, the edges held, the colours read the way the artist specified them, and the surface is on track to serve the full expected service life.

title: "Joyce Station: StreetBond public art installed at TransLink's SkyTrain concourse"
description: "Renée Van Halm's 'Carpeting' rendered in StreetBond across the Joyce–Collingwood SkyTrain concourse, installed at TransLink, notes on a transit-scale public art install."
date: "2025-10-28"
author: "Square One Paving"
category: "Public Art"
featured_image: "/images/products/streetbond/streetbond-multicolour-plaza-transit-dusk-01.jpg"
tags: ["TransLink", "SkyTrain", "StreetBond", "public art", "Vancouver", "Joyce Station"]
---

Joyce–Collingwood SkyTrain Station, Vancouver, installed at TransLink. The concourse surface carries a public art installation by Renée Van Halm, a Dutch-born, Vancouver-based artist, commissioned through TransLink's public art program. The piece runs across the pedestrian transition zones, rendered in StreetBond colour coatings.

We installed it. This is a note on what transit-scale public art actually requires on the install side.

## Why StreetBond for transit art

Public art in a SkyTrain station context is an unusual technical problem. The surface has to survive:

- Continuous pedestrian traffic including wheeled luggage and strollers
- Winter salt tracked in from the platform stairs
- Daily wet-cleaning with industrial equipment
- Seven-day-a-week operation with no scheduled resurfacing window

Paint doesn't survive that environment. Tile cracks under thermal cycling and presents a liability for slipping pedestrians. The decision to use StreetBond on this project came from the durability profile: it bonds chemically to the concrete and asphalt substrate, it carries colour through its full depth rather than on top of it, and it tolerates the cleaning regime a transit concourse requires.

## Translating artwork into pavement

The artist delivers a vision. Our job is to translate that vision into a finished surface that reads the way the artist intended from every viewing angle a commuter will experience it at.

That translation involves:

**Colour matching.** StreetBond comes in a deep palette, but custom pigments get mixed for projects like this. Every colour has to be matched to the artist's specification under natural and station lighting, both. We run sample panels on-site before the install date.

**Pattern separation.** Wet-edge transitions between colours are where an install can succeed or embarrass itself. Masking and sequencing are planned on paper before anyone's on the concourse with a roller.

**Substrate preparation.** The concrete underneath was not delivered clean. Before any colour coating goes down, the substrate gets vapour-blasted back to a uniform profile: no oil staining, no residual adhesive, no surface weakness that would show through the finished coating as a shadow.

## Working inside an operating station

Joyce Station does not close for art installations. The install happened in phased night-work blocks, outside revenue hours, with full reinstatement before the station reopened each morning.

Night work at a transit facility is a choreographed operation. We coordinated with transit dispatch, station agents, and security on a nightly basis. Equipment was staged before the last train, work happened in the two-to-three hour active window, and the site was cleared and cured enough to walk on before the first morning departures.

Every panel that went down had to be fully cure-ready before the station opened. That meant the cure window and the overnight work window had to line up exactly. A miscue on either side would have shut down the concourse, which was a non-option.

## What's there now

The concourse reads as intentional. Commuters see a surface that was designed, not defaulted into, and the art carries recognition value for the station in a way that a beige tile floor never would.

From an installer's perspective, the work that holds up at a transit site is the work where the product, the artist's brief, and the site's operational constraints were all solved simultaneously. Joyce Station is in that category.

The park opened on schedule with the refreshed surface carrying the colours the community expected to see.

This is a note on recoat work: the category of pavement-coating project that keeps civic recreation surfaces readable across their intended service life.

## What a recoat actually is

A StreetBond install has a service life in the fifteen-plus year window at full colour saturation under BC conditions. Past that window, the material is still structurally sound and still protecting the substrate, but the colour fades from its original saturation. For a recreational-use site like a spray park, where colour is part of the experience, that colour fade starts to read as tired pavement even when the underlying structure is fine.

A recoat solves the colour problem without requiring a full removal and reinstall. The existing StreetBond surface gets prepped (cleaned, any failed patches repaired) and a fresh colour layer is applied over the existing substrate. The chemistry of the StreetBond system supports this kind of layered recoat directly.

At Keswick, the recoat approach reset the surface to full-saturation colour ahead of a busy summer season, without the cost and the closure window that a full reinstall would have required.

## Why StreetBond 150 for a spray park

Spray park surfaces operate under an unusual set of stressors. The surface is wet most of the operating day. Children run, fall, and slide across it. Pool chemicals, sunscreen residue, and organic debris accumulate on the coating. Winter freeze-thaw cycles work through the surface when the park is closed.

StreetBond 150 is engineered for this environment. The coating chemistry bonds to the substrate in a way that tolerates continuous moisture. The surface profile holds slip-resistance under wet conditions. The colour palette retains saturation under continuous UV.

Paint doesn't survive a spray park environment. Tile presents safety and maintenance challenges that spray parks are specifically designed to avoid. StreetBond 150, or its equivalent in the decorative-coating category, is the standard specification for this use.

## The prep

Before the recoat colour went down, the existing surface was pressure-cleaned and inspected. Any areas of coating failure, small spots where the underlying asphalt had been exposed by wear, were repaired ahead of the colour application.

Spray parks are easier to prep than most civic sites because the park is closed during prep and the surface is designed to drain cleanly. The harder part of a spray park recoat is scheduling: the install has to happen in a window that lets the system cure fully before the summer opening, and the ambient temperature has to support that cure schedule.

At Keswick, we scheduled the install in late May, which gave the recoat roughly two weeks of cure time before the June opening. That's within the cure window StreetBond specifies, with schedule buffer in case weather required a short delay.

## The colour match

A recoat raises a particular question about colour: do you match the original install exactly, or do you refresh the palette? For Keswick, the specification called for a faithful match to the original palette. The park's character is tied to the colours the community grew up with, and the recoat was meant to restore that character rather than reinvent it.

We ran sample panels on-site before the full recoat began, matching the new colour batches against the residual saturation of the existing surface in areas the community engaged with most directly. The Parks team reviewed the samples and confirmed the match before we committed to the full install.

That step matters more than most clients realize. Colour matching on a recoat is not the same problem as colour matching on a new install: you are matching to a weathered surface, not to a specification sheet, and the panel review is the only way to confirm the match reads correctly under site lighting.

## What the park looks like now

Keswick reopened in June 2024 with the refreshed surface. The colours read at full saturation. The substrate is protected for another service window. The community engaged with the park the way it has for years, with the visual refresh landing as "the park looks good this year" rather than as an announced renovation.

That reading is the goal of a successful recoat. The community should recognize the park, not interrogate the surface. If the recoat works, the work becomes invisible, which is, of course, the opposite of how it works on an initial install.

## For parks and recreation teams

If you're a BC municipal parks or recreation team with StreetBond surfaces past their colour-saturation window, a recoat is worth evaluating before a full reinstall. The cost difference is substantial and the closure window is shorter.

Commercial Drive, Vancouver. The stretch of the Drive that Vancouverites still call Little Italy now carries crosswalks rendered in green, white, and red, the colours of the Italian flag, installed into the intersections themselves. We installed the work in TrafficPatterns preformed thermoplastic, in coordination with the Commercial Drive Business Society.

This is a note on neighbourhood-branded pavement art and why the product choice matters when the pattern is supposed to read as identity, not as paint.

## Why neighbourhood branding on the ground

Vancouver has been working for years on what urbanists call "place-identity infrastructure": the small, repeated civic gestures that tell residents and visitors what neighbourhood they are standing in. Signage is one lever. Street furniture is another. Pavement art is a third, and it is the one that most directly shapes how a neighbourhood reads from a pedestrian's eye level.

For Little Italy, the flag-colour crosswalks reinforce the identity that the Drive has carried for three generations. Vancouver's Italian community established itself along Commercial Drive in the postwar decades, and while the demographics of the Drive have broadened, the neighbourhood's Italian roots remain part of its public identity. Rendering that identity into the crosswalks is a gesture that meets the community where it has always been.

## TrafficPatterns for a crosswalk brand install

Crosswalk branding has a technical problem painted markings can't solve. The crosswalk surface takes direct vehicular loading from turning and through traffic. It takes winter salt and abrasion. It takes rain, freeze, and UV across a four-season cycle. A painted tricolour crosswalk on Commercial Drive would read beautifully on the day it was installed and would be visibly degraded within eighteen months.

TrafficPatterns solves that problem through its chemistry. The preformed thermoplastic sheets are torch-applied to the asphalt: the material fuses into the substrate rather than sitting on top of it. Colour runs through the full depth of the sheet, which means mechanical abrasion from tire contact exposes more pigmented material rather than wearing the colour off.

Expected service life on the Commercial Drive installation is in the seven-to-ten-year window at full colour saturation, with the pattern holding recognizable through the back half of that service window even as the material softens.

## Pattern layout in an active corridor

Commercial Drive does not close for pavement work. The Drive is one of Vancouver's busiest commercial corridors, with retail operating on both sides of the street and pedestrian traffic heavy through the daytime and evening hours.

We scheduled the install in coordinated overnight blocks, working intersection by intersection. Each intersection's install was sequenced so the crosswalk could be closed, prepped, marked, installed, and reopened inside the overnight window: no half-finished crosswalks left for morning traffic.

Substrate prep was the longest portion of each overnight block. The asphalt at a downtown intersection accumulates oil deposits, gum, and surface film that have to be cleared before a thermoplastic install will bond cleanly. We use mechanical and vapor-blast prep depending on the substrate condition. At each Commercial Drive intersection, we assessed the asphalt before the install team arrived with the thermoplastic sheets.

## The tricolour layout

The flag-colour crosswalks use the standard vertical tricolour (green, white, red) oriented so a pedestrian crossing the Drive walks through the stripes in sequence. The proportions are set to meet the city's crosswalk-visibility standards while preserving the recognizability of the flag pattern.

That proportional balance is the kind of decision that matters more than it seems. A tricolour pattern that reads as flag but fails the visibility standard would have been rejected by the city's engineering review. A tricolour pattern that meets the engineering standard but reads as stripes rather than flag would have failed the placemaking brief. The final layout threads both.

## What Commercial Drive reads like now

A pedestrian crossing Commercial Drive at one of the branded intersections walks across a surface that says, without any accompanying signage, that this is Little Italy. A driver approaching the intersection registers the colour blocks from half a block out, which reinforces the crosswalk's role as a safety marking as well as a placemaking gesture.

The Business Society reported stronger foot-traffic response in the months following the install, particularly around the summer festival calendar that draws visitors to the Drive. Whether that response is directly attributable to the crosswalks or to coincident programming is the kind of question a civic-economics study would have to answer, but the anecdotal evidence suggests the branded crosswalks are doing their placemaking work.

## For other BIAs and cultural districts

If you are a Business Improvement Area or cultural district in BC considering a similar install, the pattern is replicable at most scale points. The City permitting process is well-established in Vancouver and in most BC municipalities.

Memorial Park sits at the foot of a hill in White Rock, BC, where Marine Drive meets the pier and the ferries that cross to Sidney. It's a small site by the standards of urban design: perhaps four hundred square metres of public realm, plus a crosswalk that connects the parking lot to the boardwalk.

We installed the crosswalk last year. A herringbone pattern in stamped asphalt, deep terracotta colour, white margins, set into a single-lane road that becomes a pedestrian threshold for half the year. The pier is in the background of the photograph above. The Canadian flag is in the middle distance. The ferries, on a clear day, are visible just past the breakwater.

## The brief

The municipality wanted three things. They wanted the crosswalk to be obviously a crosswalk: visible from a distance, unmistakable, day or night. They wanted it to feel like part of the park, not part of the road. And they wanted it to last, because the maintenance budget for waterfront infrastructure is a serious line item.

The first two requirements are typically in tension. A crosswalk that is loud enough to be unmistakable is usually loud enough to look out of place in a heritage streetscape. The herringbone pattern in deep red was the resolution. Up close, it reads as paving: quiet, considered, of-the-place. From the approach lane, it reads as *threshold*: the colour and texture differ enough from the surrounding asphalt that a driver registers the change at a hundred metres, well before any signage triggers.

## What we used

StreetPrint imprinted asphalt with a StreetBond colour coating sealed on top. The pattern mat is a herringbone, the same brick pattern the municipality specified for several other heritage corridors, so the new install carried visual continuity with the neighbourhood's existing public realm.

The colour is a custom blend matched to the existing brick paving on the boardwalk. It will fade slightly under marine UV exposure over time, but the surface system is designed for that: colour drift on a 7-year horizon, not 7 months. We expect the install to look more or less identical in 2030.

The white border is StreetBond, applied as a separate coat after the imprint cured. It's there for two reasons. The functional reason is daytime contrast: it sharpens the crosswalk edges so drivers register the boundary at speed. The aesthetic reason is that it picks up the white of the boardwalk railings, the white of the pier columns, and the white of the flag pole. A white border is structural in design terms, not just decorative.

## What it didn't cost

The conventional alternative for a heritage crosswalk like this is real concrete pavers: laid by hand, set in mortar, requiring excavation and sub-base prep. A four-hundred-square-metre paver install in this configuration is a four-week project and runs well into six figures.

Our install was three days. The road closure was two of those days, of which one was overnight. The cost was roughly forty per cent of the paver alternative. The maintenance schedule is a colour touch-up every seven years, which is comparable to repainting a wood building.

The savings, in a municipality of White Rock's size, freed up enough of the public-realm budget to add the bollards and the lighting upgrade you can also see in the photograph. So the crosswalk did not just cost less: it *enabled* the rest of the streetscape.

## Why we like this kind of project

There is a tendency in civic design to chase the headline projects: the new transit hub, the rebuilt waterfront, the marquee bridge. Those projects matter. But the smaller surfaces (the crosswalks, the small plazas, the entry thresholds) are where a place actually announces itself to the people who use it every day.

A four-hundred-square-metre crosswalk in White Rock is not going to win an architecture prize. But it's the surface that thousands of people, every weekend, step onto when they arrive at the park. It's the threshold between the road and the boardwalk. It's the first thing the ferry passengers see when they walk up from the pier.

That kind of surface is worth getting right. So we did.

Your driveway is the first thing people see when they pull up to your home. Before they notice the fresh trim, the landscaping, or the front door, they've already formed an impression. At Square One Paving, we've been doing residential driveways across the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island for over 25 years. We've seen every condition this province can throw at a surface, and we've learned exactly what separates an install that holds up from one that doesn't.

Here's what a premium residential driveway actually looks like, and what you should expect from anyone doing this kind of work.

## BC's climate is not forgiving

The freeze-thaw cycles in the Fraser Valley. The persistent wet seasons on Vancouver Island. The weeks of standing water that pool on flat Lower Mainland lots before they have a chance to drain. This province is hard on surfaces that weren't designed for it.

We've seen driveways fail within a few years because a contractor chose the wrong product, applied it at the wrong temperature, or skipped the base assessment entirely. They look fine on day one. The cracking starts at the edges by year two. By year three, the colour has gone patchy in the UV and the repair cost is starting to look like a full redo.

A proper BC install starts before any product goes down: drainage assessment, base condition review, and choosing a system whose manufacturer publishes how it performs in wet weather, freeze-thaw and traffic.

## What we install

Depending on the condition of your existing surface, your budget, and the look you're after, there are a few directions we typically go.

**StreetBond decorative coating**

If your existing asphalt is structurally sound, StreetBond is a colour coating that changes the surface without replacing it. The chart runs to more than fifty colours, from warm terracotta to deep charcoal and slate grey, and the coating carries an anti-skid aggregate for grip underfoot. The manufacturer publishes an 8+ year life cycle, after which the surface is recoated rather than rebuilt. This is the upgrade when you want a clean, finished look without new asphalt.

**StreetPrint stamped asphalt**

This is the one that stops people on the street. StreetPrint patterns (brick, cobblestone, herringbone, slate) are pressed into the asphalt itself and coloured with StreetBond. The result looks like laid hardscape. Structurally, it's still asphalt: one continuous surface with no joints to heave, and the manufacturer publishes it as safe for snowplows and de-icing salt. Gated estate driveways, heritage homes with circular entries, townhome complexes improving their streetscape: this is where StreetPrint earns its reputation. The manufacturer publishes a 10–20 year service life for it.

**Vapour blasted surface prep**

Not every driveway needs a new surface. Sometimes it needs to be prepared properly for one. Square One runs a mobile vapour blasting service. The abrasive travels in water, so it strips old coatings, lifts stains and cleans the surface back before a new system goes down, and the dust stays on the ground: no dust cloud, no chemical residue. A cleaner result than pressure washing alone, and a better base for whatever comes next.

## The process: no surprises

We don't show up on day one with a crew and start work. Every residential job starts with a site visit.

We walk the driveway with you: checking the condition of the existing asphalt, reading the drainage patterns, flagging any structural concerns that should be addressed before a decorative system goes down. On install day the crew is Square One's own, the same crews that do our municipal work. We clean up after ourselves, and we don't disappear when the job is done: once the surface has cured, we walk the finished driveway with you.

The difference between a quality job and a budget one is rarely obvious on day one. It shows up in year three when the edges are peeling, the joints are cracking, and the surface has aged in ways that cost real money to fix.

Brighouse SkyTrain Station, TransLink's Canada Line terminus, sits at the south end of the line, where No. 3 Road in Richmond meets one of the busiest transit interchanges on the Lower Mainland. The brief was TrafficPatternsXD across the pedestrian transition zones. We installed it, and the install speaks to a different category of pavement marking than you'd spec for a residential street.

## Why TrafficPatternsXD

TrafficPatternsXD is the heaviest-duty member of the preformed thermoplastic family. Where standard TrafficPatterns is already engineered for vehicular and high-traffic pedestrian environments, the XD variant is formulated for sites that take a compounded beating: transit buses, commercial delivery vehicles, salt-tracked winter concourses, and the kind of continuous foot traffic a Canada Line terminus generates.

The pattern fuses directly into the asphalt through torch-down application. It doesn't sit on the surface the way paint does. It's structurally integrated, which is the only approach that holds up in an environment where surface abrasion is constant and scheduled maintenance windows are minimal.

## The No. 3 Road context

No. 3 Road is a primary commercial artery running the length of Richmond. Brighouse Station sits inside that context: bus bays, taxi ranks, rideshare pickups, and a pedestrian volume that doesn't let up between 5 AM and midnight.

A pavement marking at this site has to read clearly in three conditions:
- Bright midday sun reflecting off the concourse surface
- Wet overcast afternoons where contrast flattens
- Night under sodium and LED station lighting

TrafficPatternsXD carries through all three. The colour pigment runs through the full depth of the thermoplastic, not on the surface, which means UV fade and mechanical wear don't erase legibility the way they erase painted markings.

## The install

Transit sites do not close for pavement work. Our crew worked in coordinated overnight windows, staging equipment after the last revenue train, completing the install in the active window, and clearing the site before the morning service resumed.

Before the preformed sheets go down, the substrate gets assessed and prepared. Any oil, adhesive residue, or surface contamination has to be removed: a thermoplastic install over a contaminated substrate is a failed install waiting to surface. Where prep was required, we ran it in the same overnight window the install happened.

The torch-down application is straightforward once the layout is set. The crew heats the asphalt substrate and the back of the sheet simultaneously until the two bond, then rolls the sheet flush and lets it cool. The chemistry handles the rest.

## Service life at a transit site

Expected service life for TrafficPatternsXD at a high-traffic transit terminus is in the seven-to-ten-year range at full colour saturation, with gradual softening past that window. That's an order of magnitude longer than painted markings at the same site, and the maintenance overhead is proportionally lower.

At a station like this, that math matters. Painted markings at a Canada Line station would need re-striping every 12 to 18 months, which means repeated overnight closures, repeated mobilization costs, and repeated inconvenience for the operations team. A thermoplastic install trades a higher up-front cost for a service life that makes the lifecycle cost substantially lower.

## What transit agencies can take from this

If you're operating a transit facility and evaluating your pavement marking strategy, the conversation usually comes down to three questions: how long will it last, how will it read under your site conditions, and what does the install schedule look like against your operational window.

We've done transit-scale work across the Lower Mainland: Canada Line, Expo Line, SkyBridge approaches, bus exchanges. TrafficPatternsXD is the product we reach for when the site demands the top of the durability curve and the lighting conditions demand full-depth colour.

Last year we finished a full school-zone markings package at South Langford Elementary on Vancouver Island. Crosswalks, school-logo pavement graphics, speed-limit legends, and the accessible pathway lines running from the front gate to the drop-off loop.

It's the kind of project that doesn't photograph like a transit corridor or a stamped asphalt driveway. But when it's installed right, it changes how drivers behave in that zone, and for parents standing on the sidewalk in the morning, that's the measurable outcome.

## The product: preformed thermoplastic

All the coloured markings in a school zone (the yellow crosswalk bars, the blue accessible symbols, the school-crossing shields, the patterned pavement logos) come from a product family called preformed thermoplastic.

TrafficPatterns is one of the systems we install most often. It comes pre-cut in sheets. We torch-heat the surface and the sheet simultaneously, and the plastic fuses into the asphalt as it cools. Unlike paint, it doesn't sit on top of the road. It becomes part of the road.

The reason this matters at a school: paint wears thin within a winter or two. Preformed thermoplastic is far thicker and fused into the asphalt, so it keeps its colour and its retro-reflective glass beads for years rather than seasons. At a school, which handles hundreds of drop-off and pick-up cycles per week, that durability translates directly into whether a driver can still read the crosswalk at 7:30am in December rain.

## What actually slows drivers down

There's a specific combination that works in school zones:

A textured, high-contrast crosswalk bar, the yellow blocks you see laid in a ladder pattern, registers from much further out than a painted line. A driver's eye catches the pattern break before the sign does.

A pavement-logo decal, the school crest or a large school-zone shield, right before the zone. It's not just branding. It's a visual interruption. Drivers slow because the surface suddenly has information on it.

A speed-limit legend, large format, placed in-lane. Reinforces the sign. A driver who somehow missed the posted sign still reads the number on the ground.

Each of these on its own is modestly effective. Installed as a sequence, they compound.

## Why the install has to be clean

Preformed thermoplastic is an unforgiving product at install. If the asphalt underneath is damp (and in BC, especially in the shoulder seasons, it's almost always damp somewhere), the fusion doesn't happen correctly and the marking lifts within a season.

We schedule school-zone work in the dry window and we check surface moisture with a meter before any torch goes on a sheet. Not because the specification requires it, but because the alternative is a crosswalk that starts peeling at its edges by next September, with a school district asking what happened.

The actual install is also noisy, smoky, and involves open flame, so it happens outside school hours. Most of our school-zone work runs evenings or weekends, with full site cleanup before the first staff arrive.

## Specifying for a district

If you're in a BC school district looking at a summer markings refresh, or you're working with an engineering firm scoping a new school site, the decisions that matter are the material selection, the reflective-bead specification, and the crew's experience with thermoplastic at scale.

Paint is cheaper per square metre. It is not cheaper once it has been redone a few times.

blog.stamped-asphalt-vs-concrete-driveways-bc:
---
title: "Stamped asphalt vs. concrete driveways in BC"
description: "Two premium options for residential driveways. Here's the honest comparison: cost, durability, freeze-thaw performance, and what actually holds in BC."
date: "2026-01-22"
author: "Square One Paving"
category: "Residential"
featured_image: "/images/applications/private-driveways/estate-herringbone-gated-driveway-01.jpg"
tags: ["stamped asphalt", "concrete", "StreetPrint", "driveways", "West Vancouver"]
---

If you've been pricing a driveway refresh, you've run into the same comparison most BC homeowners eventually do: stamped asphalt or stamped concrete. Both produce a finished surface with pattern, colour, and curb appeal. Both carry a premium over plain black asphalt. Past that, the two are different products with different performance profiles, and in BC, the climate makes one of them a noticeably better bet.

We install stamped asphalt exclusively. We're biased, and I'll be upfront about why. But the technical case is also clear.

## The short version

Stamped concrete looks great on install day and for about five years afterward. In BC's freeze-thaw climate, the joints between the concrete slabs inevitably crack. Once water gets into a crack, every winter expands it. By year ten, most stamped concrete driveways in the Lower Mainland show pattern-level fractures that can't be patched invisibly.

Stamped asphalt (we install StreetPrint) behaves differently. Asphalt is structurally flexible. It moves with the freeze-thaw cycle instead of fighting it. The manufacturer publishes a 10–20 year service life for StreetPrint, and its StreetBond colour coat is refreshed rather than replaced when it dulls.

## What concrete does well

There's no question concrete feels premium under foot. It's rigid, the pattern is sharp, and in a dry climate it can look showroom-new for a decade.

A dry climate is the load-bearing part of that sentence.

## What happens in BC specifically

Concrete in BC deals with:

- Repeated freeze-thaw cycles through a Fraser Valley winter
- Saturated ground conditions for most of the rainy season
- Hairline cracking from thermal expansion that widens every year
- Surface scaling when de-icer chemicals react with the cement matrix

Asphalt in BC deals with the same conditions, but the material itself flexes. A stamped asphalt surface moves micro-millimetres up and down with temperature changes and settles back. Concrete can't do that: it's a rigid slab. When it wants to move and can't, it cracks.

## Install cost

Price depends on the site, the base and the pattern, so the useful comparison is two written quotes for the same driveway. The install labour is different (concrete is pour-and-stamp, asphalt is pave-and-texture).

Where the two part ways is in the years after.

Concrete typically needs a partial repair at some point. A stamped concrete driveway that develops a run of cracks is difficult to fix invisibly: matching the stamp pattern, colour, and aggregate exposure on a patch is nearly impossible. The honest options are live with visible repairs or redo the full driveway.

Stamped asphalt needs its colour coat refreshed to restore the saturation (the manufacturer publishes an 8+ year life cycle for the StreetBond coat). That's maintenance, not repair. The pattern stays intact.

## What we install

StreetPrint is the system we use for stamped asphalt driveways. Its manufacturer publishes how it performs under traffic, snowplows and de-icing salt, which is the performance that matters here. The patterns we install most often on BC properties are ashlar slate, herringbone brick, and cobblestone. They read as premium hardscape from the street and they hold up under real vehicle weight.

## Both products need base work

The biggest predictor of whether any decorative driveway holds up isn't the product on top. It's the condition of what's underneath.

We don't quote a stamped surface until we've walked the existing driveway, checked drainage, probed the asphalt base condition, and flagged any settlement issues. If the base is compromised, we say so. Installing a premium surface over a failing base just means the failure shows up sooner.

## If you're deciding

For a BC property in the Lower Mainland or on Vancouver Island, stamped asphalt is the more climate-appropriate choice. Concrete isn't wrong: it just demands a climate concrete was designed for, and we don't have that climate.

If you want a walkthrough of patterns, colours, and what would suit your specific property, we do free site visits. [Book a driveway consultation here](/contact). No pressure, and you'll leave with a clear written quote.

There is a junction on Vancouver Island that used to need three signs. A "Yield" sign for the inbound traffic. A "Pedestrian Crossing" sign for the foot traffic. A "Watch for Oncoming" warning for everyone else. Three signs, and drivers still misread the geometry.

Then we installed a brick.

Or, more accurately, we installed the appearance of brick: stamped into asphalt with a StreetPrint imprinting system, sealed in a deep terracotta colour, finished with a clean white border that rings the entire centre island. The transformation was done in a single weekend, no demolition, no road rebuild. The signs are still there. But the drivers don't need them anymore.

## What happened

The colour and texture do something that signs cannot. They tell drivers, before language has time to register, that *the road has changed*. Asphalt becomes brick. Speed becomes attention. The visual cue is processed in the part of the brain that handles environment, not the part that handles instruction. By the time a driver has decided to slow down, they have already done it.

Traffic engineers have a term for this: *self-explaining roads*. Roads designed so the appropriate behaviour is obvious from the geometry and the surface alone. Brick roundabouts are perhaps the cleanest example. The texture announces "this is a yield zone" without anyone having to read a single word.

## What we used

The roundabout surface is StreetPrint: a stamped-asphalt imprinting system. The asphalt is laid hot, the imprint mats are pressed in while it's still pliable, and the colour is applied as a heat-cured surface coating. The result is a textured surface that performs as well as plain asphalt under a snowplow blade and lasts as long as the road around it.

For the centre island, we worked with the engineering drawings to keep all crossing geometry MUTCD-compliant. The decorative treatment doesn't replace any safety markings. It *amplifies* them. The white perimeter you see in the photograph is high-friction, high-visibility coating, set against the deep red of the roundabout body so drivers register the boundary at a glance.

## What it cost

A traditional roundabout rebuild (full curb work, drainage, paver installation) is a six-figure project that closes the road for weeks. Our installation reused the existing geometry and asphalt; the entire treatment was applied to the existing road in a long weekend. The municipality booked it on a Friday afternoon and reopened on Monday morning.

For the cost of the signage budget over the next five years, the road got something signs cannot give it: a surface that says, on its own, *slow down here*.

## Why this matters for BC

Vancouver Island has a particular geography problem. Most municipalities are coastal, mountain-bordered, with corridors that funnel traffic through small junctions. The traditional fix is more signs, more lights, more lane paint. The colonial road-marking vocabulary.

Decorative pavement gives a different vocabulary. It lets the road *itself* communicate. And in a province where the views are this good, anything that quiets the visual noise of road infrastructure tends to be welcomed.

This roundabout was approved on a Tuesday. We were on site that Friday. By Monday morning, the corridor was different, and nobody had to read a thing.

blog.why-green-means-more-than-visibility.mdx:
---
title: "Why green means more than visibility"
description: "A bike lane painted green is more than visible: it's claimed. Notes from a coloured bike lane install on a BC bridge, and what colour does for cycling."
date: "2026-03-11"
author: "Square One Paving"
category: "Bike Lanes"
featured_image: "/images/applications/bike-lanes/sechelt-cowrie-and-trail-intersection-streetbond-01.jpg"
tags: ["bike lanes", "Vision Zero", "cycling infrastructure", "decorative coatings"]
---

A bike lane on a road is a line. A bike lane painted green is a *space*. The difference is not chromatic. It's territorial.

When we apply green coating to a cycling corridor (a StreetBond SR system matched to the substrate and traffic load), we are doing more than improving visibility. We are converting a graphic into a place. A driver passing the lane no longer sees a stripe and a symbol; they see a coloured zone that is no longer their road. The territory changes. So does the behaviour.

## The visibility argument is real

Let's not pretend the visibility benefit doesn't matter. It does. Coloured bike lane treatments measurably reduce conflicts at intersections, particularly during the moments of weakest perception: dawn, dusk, rain, fog. A retroreflective finish, which the manufacturer offers on StreetBond, extends the working visibility into night-time hours, which on a forested BC bridge in October is not a minor variable.

But every research synthesis that has examined coloured cycling treatments comes back with the same secondary finding: drivers don't just *see* the lane more. They *yield* the lane more. The behavioural shift is larger than the perceptual shift.

That delta is the territorial effect.

## What the colour says, before language

Drivers reading a sign make a deliberate cognitive transaction. They acquire the sign, parse the text, and decide whether to comply. The transaction takes meaningful time and is consciously revocable.

Drivers reading a colour make no such transaction. The colour bypasses linguistic processing entirely. It registers as environment, like a parking meter or a hedge or a curb, and shapes behaviour without ever asking the driver to decide. There is nothing to revoke because there was no decision in the first place.

This is the property that makes coloured cycling lanes work even with drivers who would consciously prefer not to yield. The colour decides for them, in the half-second their attention is elsewhere.

## What we install, and why

For a heavy-traffic corridor (bus rapid transit, urban arterials, BRT-adjacent cycling infrastructure), we specify the coating with the system's manufacturer for that load.

For lower-traffic urban corridors and bridge applications, StreetBond SR is the standard call. It's lighter on the substrate, applies more like a coating than a surface system, and gives us the colour palette we need for civic-scale design integration.

For a bridge cycling lane, we coordinate with the structural engineers on substrate condition, weight loading, and drainage. The coloured surface adds negligible structural load but does add a maintenance schedule: the manufacturer publishes an 8+ year life cycle for StreetBond, after which the lane is recoated rather than rebuilt, and UV exposure and traffic decide how long it runs.

## The municipality's case for green

A municipality looking at coloured cycling infrastructure is making a compound investment. Visibility, behavioural compliance, road-safety alignment, and, increasingly, *legibility for the cyclist*. A consistent green corridor across a city is something a cyclist can plan a commute around. It becomes a navigation primitive. The colour is the route.

That last property is the one we're most interested in. When the colour starts behaving like wayfinding, the cycling network gains a kind of coherence that no signage system can match. The cyclist follows the green. The driver yields the green. The colour does what the road geometry and the lane lines, on their own, never quite manage.

A bike lane on a road is a line.

A bike lane painted green is the road, claimed.
